english.html: good and weighty, as having known, haunted and frequented him from his earliest years; eaten and drunk many times with him; and the sisters, for having always been brought up together.

These witnesses, although they did not equal the number of the others, nevertheless seemed to be more credible for several considerations. The first, because they affirmed that the prisoner was Martin Guerre, and the others denied it. Now it is certain that to two witnesses alone who affirm something, more faith is given than to a thousand who deny <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>. The second, because the principal of these witnesses are his own and nearest kinsfolk: and even four sisters, who obstinately affirmed the prisoner to be their brother. And everyone knows well that kinsfolk, and singularly sisters, have without comparison a better and more perfect knowledge of those who belong to them in so near a degree of kinship than all other persons <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. The third, because the witnesses who depose for the prisoner testify to things nearer to verisimilitude. Inasmuch as he had been received as Martin Guerre by all those of the town, and even by his said sisters and nearest kinsfolk; nay, by the wife of the said Martin, with whom he had cohabited three years, and had two children: in which interval, so long, it is not probable that the said de Rols would not have recognised him for a stranger, if the prisoner had not truly been Martin Guerre. The fourth and last, because these witnesses depose for the defendant, and in favour both of the marriage and of the children who have issued from it; in which cases, if several Judges were in conflict of opinions, the opinion and judgment of those who favoured either the accused or the <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup> marriage would always prevail; and so it seems that Hermogenian the Jurisconsult wrote and taught it, when there is contradiction of witnesses. <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>

notes.citation: Accursius (Aecurſe, a wrong sort for Accurſe), the Glossa ordinaria on Digest 4.8 (De receptis: qui arbitrium receperint), l. Diem proferre, § Si plures (cf. D. 4.8.21 and D. 4.8.27, both Ulpian, on arbitrators who disagree; fragment and paragraph unverified)
notes.original: Aecurſe en la l. diem pro ferre. P. ſi plu res. D. de re cep. arb.
notes.gloss: The gloss's commonplace that two witnesses who affirm are believed before a thousand who deny, a negative not being susceptible of direct proof. The P. stands for the paragraph sign.

notes.citation: Digest 38.8 (Unde cognati), a law whose incipit the print gives as octui. — not identified (the reading is doubtful; the following p may be pr., in principio); Digest 4.1 (De in integrum restitutionibus), l. De tutela (fragment not identified)
notes.original: l. octui. p D. vnd. cog. l. de tutela. D. din integ. reſt.
notes.gloss: Cited for the knowledge kinsfolk have of their own; the print's din is de in.

notes.citation: Digest 42.1.38 pr. (De re iudicata, l. Inter pares, Paul): where judges equal in number give discordant opinions, in causes of liberty the opinion for liberty prevails (a constitution of Antoninus Pius), and in other causes that for the defendant; and a law Si in the same title (the print's c. ſi., perhaps l. fi., the last law — not identified)
notes.original: l. inter pa. res D. de re. di. c. ſi. au meſ me titre.
notes.gloss: Coras extends the favor rei of this law to the favor matrimonii.

notes.citation: Digest 40.1 (De manumissionibus), l. Lege Iulia (cf. D. 40.1.24, Hermogenian, Iuris epitomae 1; number unverified)
notes.original: l. lege iulia D. de manu miſsio.
notes.gloss: The final a of iulia is blotted. The bearing of the fragment on contradictory witnesses could not be verified.
